data.title: Course Map and How to Use This Document
data.subtitle: Math I — weeks 5–7

narr: Welcome to this comprehensive guide covering weeks 5 through 7 of Math I. This document continues the official collection 'Math I — Weeks 1–4' and includes every question and formula from each course file with complete step-by-step solutions.

The course is structured around three main weeks: Week 5 focuses on continuity and inverse functions, Week 6 covers derivatives, and Week 7 addresses related rates and exponential/logarithmic functions before the midterm review.
This guide collects materials from lectures, required readings, practical sessions, independent study assignments, and extra materials. The textbook used is OpenStax Calculus Volume 1, chapters 2-3.
Each week is organized with a formula catalog followed by questions and solutions from all source files. Problems are reproduced verbatim with complete, step-by-step solutions and checks.
The midterm exam on Monday, November 2, 2026, covers chapters 2 and 3 of the textbook, excluding subsection 3.9.3. Weeks 1-3 material is assumed known from Test 1.

Week 5 focuses on continuity and inverse functions, based on the textbook section 2.4 and instructor's notes. We'll explore the definition of continuity, types of discontinuities, and theorems on limits and composite functions.

data.heading: Definition of Continuity at a Point
bullets: A function is continuous if its graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil
Formally: f is continuous at x = a if lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a)
This requires three conditions: f(a) is defined, the limit exists, and the limit equals the function value
Equivalent form: lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = f(a)

narr: Let's start with the fundamental concept of continuity. Intuitively, a function is continuous if you can draw its graph without lifting your pencil. Formally, we say a function f is continuous at a point x = a if the limit as x approaches a of f(x) equals f(a).

This single condition actually contains three requirements: first, f(a) must be defined; second, the limit as x approaches a must exist; and third, this limit must equal the function value at a. An equivalent way to express this is that the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal to each other and to the function value at the point.

data.heading: Strategy for Checking Continuity at a Point
bullets: Step 1: Check if f(a) is defined. If not, the function is discontinuous at a
Step 2: Compute lim_{x→a} f(x). If the limit doesn't exist, the function is discontinuous at a
Step 3: Compare f(a) and lim_{x→a} f(x). If they're not equal, the function is discontinuous at a

narr: To determine if a function is continuous at a specific point, we can follow a systematic three-step strategy. First, check if f(a) is defined. If it's not, we immediately know the function is discontinuous at that point.

Second, compute the limit as x approaches a. If this limit doesn't exist (meaning it's not a real number), the function is discontinuous at a. This may require checking both the left-hand and right-hand limits separately.

Third, compare the function value f(a) with the limit. If they're not equal, the function is discontinuous at a. Only when all three conditions are satisfied can we conclude the function is continuous at that point.

data.heading: Continuity on an Interval
bullets: A function is continuous on an open interval (a, b) if it's continuous at each point in the interval
For a closed interval [a, b], the function must additionally be continuous from the right at a and from the left at b

narr: We can extend the concept of continuity from individual points to entire intervals. For an open interval (a, b), a function is continuous if it's continuous at every point within that interval.

For a closed interval [a, b], we have additional requirements. The function must be continuous from the right at point a, meaning the right-hand limit equals f(a), and continuous from the left at point b, meaning the left-hand limit equals f(b).

data.heading: Types of Discontinuities
bullets: Removable discontinuity: The limit exists but f(a) is either undefined or not equal to the limit
Jump discontinuity: Left and right limits both exist but are not equal
Infinite discontinuity: At least one one-sided limit is infinite (vertical asymptote)
Oscillatory discontinuity: The function oscillates without approaching any single value

narr: When a function is discontinuous at a point, we can classify the discontinuity into several types. A removable discontinuity occurs when the limit exists and equals some real number L, but either f(a) is undefined or f(a) ≠ L. This creates a 'hole' in the graph.

A jump discontinuity happens when both the left-hand and right-hand limits exist and are finite, but they're not equal to each other. This creates a break in the graph where the two parts don't connect.
An infinite discontinuity occurs when at least one one-sided limit is either positive or negative infinity, which typically happens at vertical asymptotes.

Finally, an oscillatory discontinuity occurs when the function oscillates as it approaches the point, never settling on any single value. A classic example is f(x) = sin(1/x) as x approaches 0, where the function oscillates infinitely rapidly.

data.heading: Continuity of Elementary Functions
bullets: Theorem 2.8: Polynomials and rational functions are continuous at each point of their domains
Theorem 2.10: Trigonometric functions are continuous on their entire domains

narr: Fortunately, many of the functions we commonly work with are continuous over their domains. According to Theorem 2.8, all polynomials and rational functions are continuous at each point in their domains.

Similarly, Theorem 2.10 tells us that all trigonometric functions are continuous on their entire domains. This means we can often assume continuity for these basic functions without having to verify the three conditions at every point.
